title: Lonely Ol' Night
description: The lead single from Scarecrow — Mellencamp's plainspoken small-town romance, filmed in and around his adopted hometown of Bloomington, Indiana.

pops.text: Lead single from Scarecrow (1985), Mellencamp's album-length tribute to the struggling American heartland.
It peaked at #6 on the Billboard Hot 100 and topped the Mainstream Rock chart in the fall of 1985.
The title was lifted from dialogue in the 1963 Paul Newman film Hud: 'It's a lonesome old night, isn't it?' — 'Ain't they all?'
The lyric name-checks the Four Tops' 1967 hit 'Standing in the Shadows of Love' — which, coincidentally, also peaked at #6.
The video was shot in and around Bloomington, Indiana, where Mellencamp has lived since the 1970s.
Mellencamp's girlfriend in the video is Kathryn Green, wife of his frequent co-writer George Green — cast after she joked that pretty girls would make the loneliness unrealistic.
Producer Don Gehman helped Mellencamp chase a raw, band-in-a-room sound modeled on 1960s rock and soul records.
The touring band behind it included guitarist Larry Crane and drummer Kenny Aronoff, Mellencamp's powerhouse rhythm man.
Mellencamp performed the song at the 1985 MTV Video Music Awards, the year Scarecrow made him a superstar.
Scarecrow reached #2 on the Billboard 200 and also gave us 'Small Town' and 'R.O.C.K. in the U.S.A.'

title: Just Kissed My Baby
description: A deep-funk masterclass from Rejuvenation (1974) — Art Neville's laid-back vocal riding one of the tightest grooves ever cut in New Orleans.

pops.text: From Rejuvenation (1974), the Meters' fifth album and their second for Reprise Records.
It was co-produced by New Orleans legend Allen Toussaint and the Meters themselves.
Recorded at Toussaint's Sea-Saint Studios in New Orleans, the band's home base through the mid-'70s.
The song was written by all four core members: Art Neville, Leo Nocentelli, George Porter Jr. and Joseph 'Zigaboo' Modeliste.
That's Art Neville singing lead — sly, relaxed, and right in the pocket.
Modeliste's drumming here is a textbook of New Orleans funk: ghost notes, drags and second-line feel in every bar.
Nocentelli's wah-soaked guitar chops against Porter's bass — the Meters' signature interlocking parts.
Rejuvenation also contains 'Hey Pocky A-Way,' the album's hit single, which reached #31 on the Hot 100.
The track found a second life with gamers: it featured on the soundtrack of Grand Theft Auto IV in 2008.
The Meters received a Grammy Lifetime Achievement Award in 2018 — this groove is a big reason why.

title: Move on Up
description: The Curtis Mayfield classic, Seattle-style: DLO3's viral KEXP performance, where a warm-up set turned a local organ trio into an international touring act.

pops.text: This is Curtis Mayfield's 1970 classic, from his solo debut Curtis — DLO3 make it the calling card of their live show.
The performance comes from KEXP in Seattle — the trio's 2017 warm-up set at the Upstream Music Festival.
KEXP's cameras happened to catch that warm-up; the video went viral, racking up millions of views and changing the band's career.
Delvon Lamarr plays a Hammond B-3 — watch for him working the bass lines on the pedals, sometimes in his socks.
Guitarist Jimmy James handles Mayfield's melody with a clean, vocal-like tone — no effects pedals in sight.
Drummer David McGraw was the trio's original drummer, from their 2015 formation in Seattle.
The KEXP session was issued on vinyl as Live at KEXP! for Record Store Day 2018 — the first KEXP session ever pressed to wax.
The trio was founded by Lamarr's wife and manager, Amy Novo, so he could focus entirely on playing.
Their debut studio album, Close but No Cigar, topped Billboard's Contemporary Jazz Albums chart.
Mayfield wrote 'Move on Up' for his 1970 solo debut Curtis, after leaving the Impressions — DLO3 stretch his nine-minute album groove into a live workout.

title: Woodstock
description: Joni Mitchell wrote it about a festival she never attended; CSNY turned it into the electric anthem of the whole era, on Déjà Vu (1970).

pops.text: Written by Joni Mitchell, who missed Woodstock itself — her manager kept her in New York for a TV appearance on The Dick Cavett Show.
Mitchell composed it in a hotel room, watching TV coverage and hearing reports from Graham Nash, her boyfriend at the time.
CSNY's version is the closing track of Déjà Vu (1970), their first album with Neil Young as a full member.
Released as a single, it reached #11 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1970.
The arrangement transforms Mitchell's quiet piano hymn into a swaggering rock track, driven by Stephen Stills' guitar and organ.
Stills sings lead, with the group's four-part harmonies stacked on the 'we are stardust' chorus.
Mitchell's own version appeared a month later on her album Ladies of the Canyon (April 1970).
Déjà Vu topped the Billboard 200 and has sold over eight million copies worldwide.
The song became so definitive that Mitchell later joked CSNY's version overshadowed her own — she reclaimed it in orchestral form decades later.
A Matthews Southern Comfort cover hit #1 in the UK in 1970 — three hit versions of one song in a single year.

title: Night Moves
description: Seger's breakthrough title track — a Michigan teenager's summer remembered by a 30-year-old man. The 1994 video, shot for his Greatest Hits, stars a pre-Friends Matt LeBlanc.

pops.text: The title track of Seger's 1976 album — the record that finally broke the Detroit rocker nationally after a decade of regional stardom.
It peaked at #4 on the Billboard Hot 100 in 1977, his first top-10 single.
Seger wrote it about a teenage romance with a girl whose boyfriend was away in the military — inspired partly by the film American Graffiti.
He labored over the song for about six months; the quiet middle breakdown was decided in the studio, late in the sessions.
Most of the album was cut in Toronto and with the Muscle Shoals Rhythm Section in Alabama — this track's band was assembled on the fly in Toronto.
This official video arrived in 1994, directed by Wayne Isham for Seger's Greatest Hits album — set in a drive-in theater in the early '60s.
Watch the young lovers: that's Matt LeBlanc, filmed just before Friends made him famous, and Daphne Zuniga of Melrose Place.
LeBlanc later claimed he shared a bottle of tequila with Seger right before the shoot.
An earlier unofficial film for the song, by Gary Weis, aired on Saturday Night Live back in January 1977.
Rolling Stone named 'Night Moves' among the 500 greatest songs of all time; the album is multi-platinum many times over.

title: Feel Like Funkin' It Up
description: The title track of Rebirth's 1989 Rounder album — the New Orleans brass band tradition rewired with funk and hip-hop swagger by the Frazier brothers' crew.

pops.text: Title track of the band's 1989 album on Rounder Records, produced by Ron Levy.
Rebirth was founded in 1983 by brothers Phil and Keith Frazier with trumpeter Kermit Ruffins, while they were still in high school.
The band grew out of marching in New Orleans parades and playing the French Quarter for tips.
Phil Frazier's tuba — 'Tuba Phil' — drives the bass line, the anchor of the modern brass band sound.
Kermit Ruffins, later a star in his own right, was an original member and sings and plays trumpet on this era's records.
Rebirth fused traditional brass band repertoire with funk and early hip-hop — a revolution younger New Orleans bands still follow.
Their Tuesday-night residency at Uptown's Maple Leaf Bar became one of the great standing gigs in American music.
The band became nationally familiar through HBO's Treme, where their music and performances recur throughout the series.
Rebirth won the Grammy for Best Regional Roots Music Album in 2012, for Rebirth of New Orleans.
The chant-along title became the band's mission statement — every show is built to feel like a second-line parade.

title: Once in a Lifetime
description: David Byrne's ecstatic midlife-crisis sermon over an Afrobeat-built groove — and one of MTV's defining early videos, co-directed by Toni Basil, all twitches, trances and multiple Byrnes.

pops.text: From Remain in Light (1980), the band's fourth album, built from studio jams inspired by Fela Kuti's Afrobeat.
Co-written by all four Heads plus producer Brian Eno, who looped their improvisations into song structures at Compass Point Studios in the Bahamas.
Tina Weymouth's bass line is the foundation — the whole track extrapolates from her riff.
Byrne's vocal was inspired by radio preachers; he half-sings, half-testifies the 'same as it ever was' litany.
As a single it stalled at #103 in the US but hit #14 in the UK — America caught up via MTV.
The video was co-directed by Toni Basil — yes, of 'Mickey' fame — and Byrne, using bluescreen to multiply him against a white void.
Byrne and Basil studied footage of preachers, religious rituals and people in trances to build his jerky, possessed choreography.
MTV launched six months after the single; the low-budget video went into heavy rotation and became iconic.
The live version in Jonathan Demme's Stop Making Sense (1984), with Byrne in the oversized suit, is nearly as famous as the video.
Rolling Stone ranked it among the greatest songs of all time, and the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame lists it among the songs that shaped rock.

title: Fire Woman
description: The lead single from Sonic Temple (1989) — producer Bob Rock polishing Ian Astbury and Billy Duffy's goth-rock roots into pure arena thunder.

pops.text: Lead single from Sonic Temple (1989), the Cult's fourth album and their commercial peak.
Written by singer Ian Astbury and guitarist Billy Duffy, the band's founding partnership.
Produced by Bob Rock — just before he turned Metallica into stadium giants with the Black Album.
It reached #46 on the Billboard Hot 100, while Sonic Temple itself hit #10 on the album chart — both career highs for the band at the time.
Duffy's Gretsch White Falcon and that opening riff — the Cult fully embracing big American hard rock.
The album was recorded in Vancouver, Rock's home turf, with session drummer Mickey Curry behind the kit.
Sonic Temple spun off four singles: this, 'Edie (Ciao Baby)', 'Sun King' and 'Sweet Soul Sister.'
The Cult had started the decade as a gothic post-punk band, Southern Death Cult, before shedding names and sounds en route to this.
Astbury's 'fire woman' is a classic femme fatale — the lyric is pure lust and danger, delivered like a revival preacher.
The song has stayed a fixture of the band's live sets ever since — their signature show-opener energy in five minutes.

title: Dirty Paws
description: The opening track of My Head Is an Animal — an Icelandic folk fable about a war between birds and beasts, told in the band's official lyric video starring a flag-bearing giant crossing a mountainscape.

pops.text: Opening track of the band's debut album, My Head Is an Animal, first released in Iceland in 2011.
The album's title comes from a line in this very song: 'Jumping up and down the floor, my head is an animal.'
Written by co-singers Nanna Bryndís Hilmarsdóttir and Ragnar Þórhallsson — the band's boy-girl vocal trade-off starts here.
The lyric is a fairy tale: a beast with four dirty paws, a forest war between birds and bees, and a petrified forest left behind.
Released as a single in April 2012, it reached #19 on Billboard's Alternative Songs chart in 2013 — a slow-burn American breakthrough.
The official lyric video (2014), directed by WeWereMonkeys, follows a two-legged creature carrying a flag through Icelandic mountains as phoenix-like birds swarm.
The song reached global ears on the trailer and soundtrack of The Secret Life of Walter Mitty (2013), also set partly in Iceland.
It later turned up in the first episode of Netflix's Sweet Tooth (2021).
The band formed in Reykjavík in 2010 and won Iceland's national battle-of-the-bands, Músíktilraunir, the same year.
My Head Is an Animal eventually went platinum in the US on the back of 'Little Talks' — but this is the track that opens the story.

title: Kiss Off
description: Track two of the Femmes' 1983 debut — Gordon Gano's teenage neediness flipping into a counting-down tantrum, performed here live in WFUV's Studio A in 2015.

pops.text: Second track on Violent Femmes (1983), the Milwaukee trio's debut — sequenced to explode right after 'Blister in the Sun.'
Gordon Gano wrote the album's songs while still in high school; the adolescent ache is entirely authentic.
The famous breakdown counts off everything he gave her — 'one, one, one for the money' — up to eight, 'for everything, everything.'
Brian Ritchie's acoustic bass guitar does the work of an entire rhythm section — huge, funky and percussive.
Victor DeLorenzo's minimalist kit — brushes on a snare and a tranceaphone made from a tomato can — defined the band's folk-punk sound.
The debut was recorded for Slash Records in July 1982 and initially sold slowly, building by word of mouth into a platinum cult classic.
The Femmes were discovered playing on a Milwaukee street corner by James Honeyman-Scott of the Pretenders, who got them an opening slot that night.
Matt Berninger of The National lifted its 'they can all just kiss off into the air' spirit — and a line — into 'Hard to Find.'
This performance was recorded live at WFUV in New York on May 20, 2015, during the band's reunion era.
The debut album never charted high, yet the RIAA certified it platinum in 1991 — eight years after release.

title: Tomorrow People
description: Bob Marley's kids ask where the tomorrow people are going — the Conscious Party breakthrough single, produced by Talking Heads' Chris Frantz and Tina Weymouth, with its very-'80s MTV video.

pops.text: From Conscious Party (1988), the album that made Bob and Rita Marley's children stars in their own right.
It reached #39 on the Billboard Hot 100 — a bigger US pop hit than any single Bob Marley himself ever had.
Conscious Party won the Grammy for Best Reggae Album in 1989.
The album was produced by Chris Frantz and Tina Weymouth of Talking Heads, their first outside production — they brought a pop sheen to the Marley sound.
The Melody Makers are siblings: Ziggy with sisters Sharon and Cedella and younger brother Stephen, who takes a lead vocal turn on the album.
Talking Head Jerry Harrison guests on Hammond B-3 organ on this track.
Keith Richards also guests elsewhere on the album — the Stones were longtime Marley admirers.
The group formed when Ziggy was 11; the siblings had sung at their father's funeral in 1981.
The sunny video put the family into MTV rotation — reggae-pop aimed squarely at the mainstream, and it worked.
Ziggy wrote it as a genuine question to his generation: 'Where is your love?' — the Marley family business of hopeful protest.

title: Support Your Local Emperor
description: A nine-minute Travelers and Thieves epic — John Popper's harmonica and rapid-fire wordplay in service of a tongue-in-cheek hymn to a hometown tyrant, a longtime live showpiece.

pops.text: From Travelers and Thieves (1991), Blues Traveler's second album for A&M Records.
Written by bassist Bobby Sheehan and John Popper — Sheehan's music with Popper's torrent of lyrics.
Running around nine minutes on the album, it's a jam vehicle: in concert it routinely stretched past ten.
The lyric is satire — a subjects'-eye tribute to a petty emperor who holds everyone's fate at his fingertips.
Popper's harmonica playing redefined the instrument for rock: fast, amplified runs through a special microphone setup of his own design.
The band formed in Princeton, New Jersey, in 1987 — Popper and drummer Brendan Hill had been playing together since high school.
Travelers and Thieves was produced by Jim Gaines, known for his work with Santana and Stevie Ray Vaughan.
Blues Traveler were pillars of the early-'90s jam scene and co-founded the H.O.R.D.E. festival tour in 1992.
Bassist Bobby Sheehan, who co-wrote this song, died in 1999; the band dedicated their album Bridge to him and carried on with Tad Kinchla on bass.
A live version anchors the band's 2003 concert film Live — Thinnest of Air, where the song runs a full nine-plus minutes.

title: Don't Think Twice, It's All Right
description: Dylan's elegant kiss-off from The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan (1963) — one take, Bruce Langhorne's filigree guitar, and a melody borrowed from his friend Paul Clayton.

pops.text: From The Freewheelin' Bob Dylan (1963), his breakthrough second album, and released as his second-ever single that August.
Dylan recorded it in a single take on November 14, 1962, at Columbia's Studio A in New York, produced by John Hammond.

The melody derives from the traditional 'Who's Gonna Buy Your Chickens When I'm Gone,' taught to Dylan by folksinger Paul Clayton, who'd used it in his own 'Who's Gonna Buy You Ribbons When I'm Gone.'
That debt caused friction: Clayton's publisher sued, and the matter was settled out of court — the friendships survived.
The delicate fingerpicked accompaniment is guitarist Bruce Langhorne, not Dylan — Dylan plays the rhythm behind him.
It was written as his girlfriend Suze Rotolo extended her stay in Italy; she's the woman walking with him on the Freewheelin' album cover.
Peter, Paul and Mary took their cover to #9 on the Hot 100 in 1963, making Dylan a bankable songwriter before he was a hit singer.
The Four Seasons, recording as The Wonder Who?, took a novelty version to #12 in 1965.
Dylan's own liner notes describe it as 'a statement that maybe you can say to make yourself feel better... as if you were talking to yourself.'
It remains one of his most covered songs — hundreds of versions, from Johnny Cash to Eric Clapton to Kesha.

title: Magic Bus
description: Pete Townshend's one-chord Bo Diddley bus ride — written in 1965, released in 1968, and a live staple the band stretched into a jamming vehicle, as in this 1968 performance.

pops.text: Townshend wrote it in 1965, around the time of 'My Generation' — but the band held it back for three years.
It was finally released as a single in 1968, reaching #26 in the UK and #25 on the US Billboard Hot 100.
The whole song rides essentially one chord over a Bo Diddley beat, with claves keeping the rhythm up front.
The narrator spends 'thruppence and sixpence every day' riding that bus to his girlfriend's house — and spends the song trying to buy it outright.
A US compilation album, Magic Bus: The Who on Tour, took its name from the song the same year.
Townshend has called it one of his favorite songs to play live because of the rhythm — live versions stretched toward eight minutes, as heard on Live at Leeds.
Bassist John Entwistle disagreed: he complained that playing one note for eight minutes could make him sound half asleep.
The demo was so strong that Townshend said the band long hesitated to record it, pressuring producer Kit Lambert to better it.
The song's title later adorned a real custom VW bus, raffled for Roger Daltrey's Teenage Cancer Trust charity.
An eager bidder in the lyric offers 'thruppence and sixpence' — pre-decimal British pocket change, for a psychedelic bus.

title: Wild Night
description: The opening track of Tupelo Honey (1971) — Ronnie Montrose's guitar and one of pop's great bass lines launching Van's most joyful single, all wild night breezes and dancing in the street.

pops.text: Opening track and lead single from Tupelo Honey (1971), Morrison's fifth studio album.
Released in September 1971, it reached #28 on the Billboard Hot 100.
The released version was recorded in spring 1971 at Wally Heider Studios in San Francisco, produced by Ted Templeman.
An earlier attempt dates to autumn 1968 in New York with producer Lewis Merenstein — Morrison re-cut it for Tupelo Honey.
That's future Montrose and Van Halen sideman Ronnie Montrose playing the lead guitar lines.
Bassist Bill Church's bouncing line is the engine — often cited among the most infectious bass parts in pop.
Tupelo Honey was written during a happy domestic spell in Woodstock, New York, before Morrison relocated to California to record it.
Martha Reeves covered it in 1974 for her debut solo album, giving it a full Motown-soul reading.
John Mellencamp and Meshell Ndegeocello's 1994 duet cover became a #3 Hot 100 hit — bigger on the charts than Van's original.
Morrison still performs it in concert more than fifty years on; it closed the book on his early-'70s run of perfect singles alongside 'Domino' and 'Tupelo Honey.'
